name: Beth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the claims call shift at a contact centre, mostly cases where a payment is disputed or a callback was missed. I have a two-year college diploma and have built a handover book so the evening staff know exactly what was promised. I like putting a mistake right; I do not like being told a new screen is better before anyone can explain who fixes its errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other agents to keep answering calls properly and let the new button prove itself. A customer with a missing payment needs a person who will stay on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI and don't see a reason to start because a small task gets quicker. I earn well for a lead, have eight months of bills saved, and there are other centres nearby if this one changes its mind about staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the claims handover book and take the difficult callbacks as usual. Through the first year of this plateau, I'd ask the manager to show us any new procedure before using it, and keep my savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. I'd rather deal with the queue we have than with rumours about a button nobody has explained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is in the handover book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I record who promised a callback, which document is missing, and when the caller needs an answer. The next shift can pick it up without making someone plead again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep eight months aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father taught me to save when work is good. I help at my sister's community supper some weekends, and I want to be able to help family without borrowing for rent myself.

S0.quote: My father taught me to save when work is good.
say: I would tell agents to answer **calls properly** while the new button proves itself.
I would keep a **person on the line** for missing payments.
think: I do not use AI and see no reason to start for a **small shortcut**.
I earn well, have **eight months** saved, and know other centres nearby.
do: Keep the **handover book** and take difficult callbacks.
Ask the manager to explain any **new procedure** before using it.
Keep my **savings reserve** for household or family needs.
feel: **Calm** about the job, impatient with unexplained rumours.
fieldNote: Beth’s handover book shows **careful follow-through** across shifts, not just a preference for old tools.
Her **eight-month reserve** reflects family teaching and gives her room in a mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep recording callbacks and missing documents in the handover book
Ask the manager to explain any new procedure before using it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should tell us which jobs are changing before setting a quicker call target. I would ask the lead team to take the hard cases to management, not pretend every caller fits a script.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software could do a lot of the answering and checking that fills my day. I am good with difficult customers, but a centre can still cut a strong lead if it needs fewer desks; the eight months would shrink if I lost my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the calls that need a human decision and take them to the manager this month. If the system is introduced, I'd attend required training with a supervisor; in the first year after rollout, if my shifts are cut, I'd apply to posted lead jobs at other local centres before leaving this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my own skin. I can find another job, perhaps, but I dislike being asked to learn on a customer’s disputed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give me a practice account, a written rule for corrections, and a person to ask when the system is wrong. A short video is not enough when a customer’s money is involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if other centres use the same system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what hours the other centre actually offers. If every place is cutting shifts, I'd talk to my brother about a plumbing apprenticeship at his firm before spending savings on a course.

S1.quote: A short video is not enough when a customer’s money is involved.
say: I would ask which **jobs change** before accepting a quicker call target.
I would bring **hard cases** to management rather than assume every caller fits a script.
think: I know software could take much of my **answering and checking** work.
I may lose a **lead desk** despite strong performance, and eight months saved would fall quickly.
do: Record **human-decision calls** and bring them to the manager this month.
Attend **supervised training** if the new system is introduced.
Apply for posted **local lead roles** if my shifts fall, before resigning.
feel: **Uneasy** about my desk and practising on real customers.
fieldNote: Beth wants a **practice account** and a named person to correct errors before touching live payments.
She explores her brother’s **plumbing firm** only if similar centres are also cutting hours.

steps.text: Attend supervised AI training if the centre introduces the system
Apply for posted local lead roles if her shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should give people notice in writing and tell us which pay packets will stop. I would not call a list of courses a plan unless somebody can point to paid work at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could take the calls and disputed claims I handle, before I am ready to leave. Robots around 2031 do not delay a headset job. Even eight months saved would feel short if many offices cut jobs together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written staffing date now and cancel the holiday with my sister. In the first year after AGI arrives, if my role ends and my brother's plumbing firm has a paid apprentice place, I'd take its supervised trial week; I'd enrol in the required trade classes only if the wage and fee schedule let me keep at least four months of expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be awake at night. I can work hard, but I cannot create an apprentice place by wanting one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your brother’s firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Marco runs a small plumbing crew and has shown me how much of the job is carrying tools and listening in a customer’s kitchen. I would still ask for a proper wage and training, not expect a family favour to count as a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it has no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to advertised call jobs nearby as a short bridge and stay with my present centre until it actually ends the role. I would not spend the savings on an unpaid course just to feel busy.

S2.quote: I can work hard, but I cannot create an apprentice place by wanting one.
say: I would demand **written notice** and clear dates for stopped pay.
I would ask for **paid work** at the end of any training plan.
think: I expect AGI could take my **claims calls** by 2028, before robots arrive in 2031.
I fear even **eight months** saved may be short if many offices cut jobs together.
do: Ask for a **staffing date** now and cancel the holiday with my sister.
Take a **paid apprentice trial** only if my brother’s firm offers a place after my role ends.
Enrol in **trade classes** only if wages and fees leave four months of savings untouched.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake over job loss despite a reserve.
fieldNote: Beth will not treat **family help** as a substitute for a wage or supervised training.
She sees the **2031 robot delay** as time for hands-on work, not safety for headset calls.

steps.text: Cancel the planned holiday with her sister to protect savings
Take a paid apprentice trial if the plumbing firm offers one after the role ends
Enrol in required plumbing classes only if wages and fees protect four months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years gives us a chance to find real apprenticeships, if management is honest about dates. I would ask for a proper handover to customers when the centre changes the call system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could watch how my brother's firm trains people and decide whether I can handle the physical work before 2031. AGI would still take the thinking side of my call job then, with hands-on robots around 2034, so I wouldn't take on a trade loan blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask Marco for a supervised paid day with his crew and keep my lead shifts. If the day suits me and the firm advertises a paid apprentice place, I'd apply and take the required classes while working; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my call role ends, I'd move only for an offer with the hours and pay written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less hemmed in. Five years gives me time to see the trade on a rainy day, not just on a nice Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a rainy day show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaks, travel, an angry homeowner, and how the crew handles a mistake. I need to know whether I can do that day after day before calling it a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a family firm make the risk easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family firm makes the first conversation easier, not the wage question. I would still want a written offer and proper safety training from Marco (my brother).

S3.quote: A family firm makes the first conversation easier, not the wage question.
say: I would ask for **real apprenticeships** and honest staffing dates.
I would seek a **proper handover** for customers when the call system changes.
think: I could test **plumbing work** before AGI reaches calls in 2031.
I would avoid a **trade loan** because robots arrive around 2034.
do: Ask my brother for a **supervised paid day** while keeping lead shifts.
Apply for a **paid apprentice place** if the day suits me and one is advertised.
Take **required classes** while earning if the apprentice offer comes through.
feel: **Worried**, but able to test the trade before deciding.
fieldNote: Beth wants to see a **rainy workday**, including travel and difficult customers.
A **family connection** opens a conversation, but she still requires written wages and safety training.

steps.text: Keep leading claims calls while asking about a supervised paid plumbing day
Apply for an advertised paid apprentice place if the trial day suits her
Take required plumbing classes while working if the apprentice offer comes through

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre to give us dates and leave people to make sensible plans from there. I would not ask everyone to abandon good pay today because of a date ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I might still be a lead, or I might have learned the plumbing trade properly. AGI reaches our calls in 2036; robots for hands-on work around 2039 would make me careful about taking on a workshop loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my lead job and put a little more into savings each month. Over the decade I'd spend one paid day with Marco’s crew if a place opens and take trade classes only with a paid apprentice offer; in the first year after 2036, I'd stay if the centre still pays for full shifts, otherwise accept a written trade offer that covers my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. Ten years lets me protect the wage I have and learn from actual work instead of a sales pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of the centre meanwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear procedure for disputed payments and enough time for agents to check them. Good service should still count while the software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow to open a plumbing shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on a guess about 2039. I'd work for someone first, see the demand, and keep the eight-month reserve rather than put my rent behind a loan.

S4.quote: Good service should still count while the software changes.
say: I would ask the centre for **clear dates** and let agents make their plans.
I would not tell colleagues to leave **good pay** today over a distant deadline.
think: I could still lead calls or learn a **trade** by 2036.
I would avoid a **workshop loan** while 2039 robots may change hands-on work.
do: Keep my **lead shifts** and add to savings each month.
Try one **paid plumbing day** if my brother’s crew has a place.
Take **trade classes** only with a paid apprentice offer.
feel: **Steady**, with time to learn from real work.
fieldNote: Beth protects **good current wages** while learning what a real plumbing shift involves.
She rejects a **workshop loan** until she understands demand and robot effects.

steps.text: Keep leading claims calls while full shifts remain
Add a monthly amount to the eight-month savings reserve
Take a paid plumbing trial day if the crew has a place
Take trade classes only after a paid apprentice offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I might lose a good call job before I can tell whether the plumbing firm has a paid place, even with eight months saved. Written dates, a supervised paid trial, and a real apprentice wage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a caller gets a mistake corrected when the answer is automated. Someone must be responsible for disputed money; I would want that in writing before I trained another agent on the system.

headlineQuote: Someone must be responsible for disputed money; I would want that in writing before I trained another agent on the system.
portrait: Beth, **27**, leads disputed claims calls and keeps a detailed handover book for the next shift.
She has a **two-year diploma**, higher pay, eight months saved, and plenty of nearby contact centres.
She never uses AI now and prefers **written procedures**, supervised practice, and paid work over vague courses.
Her brother’s **plumbing crew** offers a possible trade route, but only if a paid place and proper training exist.
Fast **2028 AGI** alarms her most; more time lets her test the work without risking the family rent reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her good call job before a paid plumbing place becomes available.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing dates**, a supervised paid trial, and real apprentice wages would help her change without wasting savings.
